quote: How are you doing today? Got no form. I'm in got no form.
stewart_read: The customer denies recognizing the form immediately, and the rep's recovery ('I've got it here for a 1320 Greta Boulevard') doesn't resolve the legitimacy question — it just restates the address, which the customer also doesn't confirm clearly.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to anchor legitimacy with a clear, specific lead-source statement (e.g., date/site the form was filled) rather than just repeating an address the customer hasn't confirmed.

quote: Right. Yeah. I'm I'm just curious why that is. All they do is replace your current power bill with something cheaper, so it's saving money every month.
stewart_read: This is unsolicited feature-selling ('all they do is...') in response to a flat refusal, rather than a curiosity-creating question about the customer's own bill or usage. This invites exactly the mechanism debate that follows.
coaching_implication: Replay this line with the rep — the move to make here is asking about the customer's own bill instead of asserting a generic savings claim.

quote: No. Not at all. I mean, it's replacing your current electric bill.
stewart_read: Customer's neighbor-anecdote objection is a classic cost-skepticism trigger. Instead of flipping it toward the customer's own bill pain, the rep argues the mechanism directly, which keeps the conversation on the customer's chosen (losing) ground.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read: rep is simply trying to correct a factual misunderstanding, not missing a strategic flip. This is plausible but the correction doesn't move the call forward — it just restates the same claim already rejected, supporting the objection_inversion_miss read as the stronger one.
coaching_implication: Show the rep the schema's flip patterns (e.g., redirecting to what the customer's OWN bill costs) rather than arguing a neighbor's unverifiable situation.

quote: Okay. Do you know if the solar is covering all of his electric needs or just parts or I don't know.
stewart_read: Rep admits uncertainty ('or I don't know') on the same neighbor-anecdote thread she had flatly denied two exchanges earlier ('No. Not at all.'). The inconsistency signals the rep was improvising the rebuttal rather than working from a clear framework.
coaching_implication: Point out the contradiction between the 01:23 denial and the 02:19 admission of not knowing — the rep needs one consistent, honest answer, not two different postures on the same claim.

quote: Are you with the Valley Electric? Is that your power provider?
stewart_read: The utility-company qualifier — a basic, early verify item that would have surfaced the DQ immediately — is asked only after nearly two and a half minutes of unproductive feature debate. This isn't a probe-miss on competitive intel; it's a sequencing failure that let a losing conversation run far longer than necessary.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: rep may have been trying to keep the customer engaged long enough to build rapport before qualifying. Not supported — the exchanges (01:56, 02:33) show escalating customer frustration, not warming, so continuing the debate had no strategic payoff.
coaching_implication: Coach sequencing: run the utility-company verify question early, before investing time defending solar's economics to a resistant customer.

quote: Gotcha. So I actually know that we we don't work with Valley Electric anyway. So I'll just take you off my list here. I appreciate your time.
stewart_read: Call ends with a flat DQ statement and no attempt to leave the door open (e.g., no mention of alternative options, no button-up language). Given the DQ is legitimate (out of service area), the exit itself is appropriate, but it is abrupt after a contentious exchange.
coaching_implication: Not a high-priority fix given the DQ is valid, but note for the rep that closing lines should stay calm and neutral regardless of how the prior exchange went.
